---
title: "Coming from robotstxt"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(robotstxtr)
```

This article is for users of the CRAN package `robotstxt` who are moving
to robotstxtr. It covers three things: which robotstxtr function
replaces each `robotstxt` function, the cases where the two packages give a
different allow or disallow answer for the same file, and what robotstxtr
offers that `robotstxt` does not.

Everything said here about `robotstxt` refers to version 0.7.15, as its
help pages and `NEWS.md` describe it. robotstxtr does not depend on
`robotstxt`, and this article never runs it. The answers quoted for
`robotstxt` come from the library comparison recorded in the repository,
[`design/library-comparison.md`](https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr/-/blob/main/design/library-comparison.md),
which ran both packages on the same synthesized files. Each difference
below names its class there.

## Function mapping

### Checking paths

`robotstxt` checks *paths* against a *domain*; robotstxtr checks *full
URLs*. `allowed_by_robots_url()` needs each URL to start with `http://` or
`https://`, since it fetches `robots.txt` from that origin. Build URLs from
your paths before switching:

```{r}
paths <- c("/", "/private/report")
urls <- paste0("https://example.com", paths)
urls
```

| `robotstxt` 0.7.15 | robotstxtr |
|---|---|
| `paths_allowed(paths, domain, bot)`, which fetches the file | `allowed_by_robots_url(url, user_agent)` |
| `paths_allowed(paths, domain, bot, robotstxt_list = ...)`, with text you already hold | `allowed_by_robots_text(robots_txt, url, user_agent)` |
| `robotstxt(domain = ...)`, then `$check(paths, bot)` | `allowed_by_robots_url(url, user_agent)` |
| `robotstxt(text = ...)`, then `$check(paths, bot)` | `allowed_by_robots_text(robots_txt, url, user_agent)` |

The `bot` argument becomes `user_agent`: the product token that selects the
`User-agent` group, such as `"FooBot"` or `"Googlebot"`. robotstxtr has no
default for it, where `robotstxt` uses `bot = "*"`. Pass the name of your
crawler. `robots_txt` is one string; if you hold the file as a vector of
lines, join it with `paste(lines, collapse = "\n")` first.

`paths_allowed()` returns a logical vector. robotstxtr returns a
`robots_decisions` object; the logical answer is its `results$allowed`
column, and `results$decision_source` says why:

```{r}
robots <- "User-agent: *
Disallow: /private
"

x <- allowed_by_robots_text(robots, urls, "FooBot")
x$results$allowed
x$results[c("url", "allowed", "decision_source")]
```

`allowed` can also be `NA`, when no safe answer exists: an invalid URL, a
fetch that failed, or a refused address. Treat `NA` as "do not know", not
as an allow.

The URL is matched exactly as you pass it. robotstxtr does not escape,
decode or clean it; pass a percent-encoded URL (see the raw non-ASCII
example below).

### Fetching and reading the file

| `robotstxt` 0.7.15 | robotstxtr |
|---|---|
| `get_robotstxt(domain)` | `robots_fetch(url)`, whose `robots$body` holds the raw bytes; or `robots_body()` on the result of `allowed_by_robots_url()` |
| `get_robotstxts(domain)` | `robots_fetch(url)`, which is vectorized and fetches each distinct origin once |
| `get_robotstxt_http_get(domain)` | no public equivalent; `robots_fetch()` is the fetch stage |
| `rt_last_http` | the `robots` table that `robots_fetch()` returns: `http_status`, `fetch_outcome`, `content_type` and the stored body per origin |
| `rt_request_handler()`, `request_handler_handler()` and the `on_*_default` handlers | no equivalent; see below |

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Not evaluated: these calls make network requests.
fetched <- robots_fetch(c("https://example.com/", "https://example.com/private"))
fetched$robots[c("robots_url", "fetch_outcome", "http_status")]
rawToChar(fetched$robots$body[[1]])

decisions <- allowed_by_robots_url("https://example.com/", "FooBot")
robots_body(decisions, n = Inf)
```

The fetch arguments map as follows:

| `robotstxt` argument | robotstxtr |
|---|---|
| `user_agent` (the HTTP header) | `fetch_user_agent`; `NULL` sends `robotstxtr/<version>` |
| `force`, and the session cache | none: no cache across calls, and each call fetches each origin once |
| `ssl_verifypeer` | none: TLS is always verified with the platform defaults |
| `use_futures` | none: origins are fetched one after another |
| `encoding` | none: the body's bytes are matched as received, with NUL bytes dropped |
| `warn`, `verbose` | none: fetch outcomes are columns, not warnings |
| `on_server_error`, `on_not_found`, `on_redirect` and the other handlers | a fixed policy in `allowed_by_robots_url()`; per-engine status rules in `robots_evaluate_url_v1()` |

`robotstxt` lets you pass handlers that decide what a server error, a
redirect or an HTML body means. robotstxtr does not take handlers. Its
headline functions apply one documented policy: a 404 or 410 allows
(`missing_allow`), and any other failure gives `NA` (`fetch_unknown`). When
you need a search engine's own reading of a status code, use the engine
rulesets described at the end of this article. A body that looks like HTML,
XML or JSON is still matched as it is; `robots_fetch()` reports the guess in
its `content_flag` column.

### Parsing and validity

| `robotstxt` 0.7.15 | robotstxtr |
|---|---|
| `parse_robotstxt(txt)` | no equivalent; robotstxtr does not return a parsed rule table |
| `robotstxt()$bots`, `$permissions`, `$sitemap`, `$host`, `$other` | no equivalent; `robots_validate_text()` reports counts and per-line diagnostics |
| `is_valid_robotstxt(text)` | `robots_validate_text(robots_txt)`, its `documents$validation_status` |
| `print()` and `as.list()` methods | `print()` methods for each result object; the results are plain lists of data frames |
| `%>%` (re-exported from `magrittr`) | not re-exported; use the base pipe `|>` |

robotstxtr does not expose a parsed rule table because it does not parse
the file in R. The vendored matcher reads the file, and robotstxtr reports
which rule decided each URL:

```{r}
m <- allowed_by_robots_text(robots, "https://example.com/private/report", "FooBot")
m$results[c("matched_line", "matched_rule_type", "matched_rule_value")]
```

## Differences that change an answer

robotstxtr follows the Google matcher it vendors. `robotstxt` 0.7.15
answers through the `spiderbar` package (its `NEWS.md` for 0.6.0 makes the
`spiderbar` check "the default and only method"). The library comparison
found the classes below, where the two give a different answer on the same
file and URL.

Each example runs live with robotstxtr. The examples use this helper, which
turns paths into URLs on `example.com` and keeps the columns that matter:

```{r}
decide <- function(body, paths, token = "FooBot") {
  x <- allowed_by_robots_text(body, paste0("https://example.com", paths), token)
  data.frame(
    path = paths,
    allowed = x$results$allowed,
    decision_source = x$results$decision_source
  )
}
```

### A line between two `User-agent` lines

`User-agent` lines in a row share one group. A `Crawl-delay` or `Sitemap`
line between them does not end the run, so `FooBot` below gets the
`User-agent: *` rules:

```{r}
stacked <- "User-agent: FooBot
Crawl-delay: 5

User-agent: *
Disallow: /x
"
decide(stacked, "/x")

stacked_sitemap <- "User-agent: FooBot
Sitemap: https://example.com/s.xml

User-agent: *
Disallow: /x
"
decide(stacked_sitemap, "/x")
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 allows `/x` in both: it ends `FooBot`'s group at the
`Crawl-delay` or `Sitemap` line and leaves it with no rules. RFC 9309 §2.2.4
also says a Sitemap line must not end a group. (Class 1.)

### Ties go to `Allow`

When an `Allow` and a `Disallow` match with the same length, `Allow` wins,
whatever their order. A trailing `*` counts toward a rule's length:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /x\nAllow: /x\n", "/x")
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /p\nAllow: /p*\n", c("/p", "/px"))
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 disallows all three: the first rule wins a tie, and it
drops the trailing `*`, which makes the second file a tie too. (Class 10.)

### `$` and `*` in patterns

```{r}
# "/*$" matches every path.
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /*$\n", c("/", "/anything"))

# A "$" that is not last is a literal character.
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /a$*\n", c("/a", "/a$", "/a$b"))

# A pattern not led by "/" or "*" never matches.
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: $\n", "/")
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 allows `/` and `/anything` under `/*$` (class 5). Under
`/a$*` it disallows `/a` and allows `/a$` and `/a$b` (class 6). It
disallows `/` under `Disallow: $`, reading the rule as `/$` (class 8).

### `Allow: /index.html` also allows the directory

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /\nAllow: /index.html\n", c("/", "/x"))
```

Google treats an allowed `index.html` or `index.htm` as allowing its
directory too, so `/` is allowed. `robotstxt` 0.7.15 disallows `/`. RFC
9309 has no such rule. (Class 22.)

### A rule before the first `User-agent`

```{r}
decide("Disallow: /x\nUser-agent: *\nDisallow: /y\n", c("/x", "/y"))
```

robotstxtr ignores a rule that comes before any `User-agent` line, so `/x`
is allowed. `robotstxt` 0.7.15 adds it to the `*` group and disallows `/x`.
(Class 19.)

### The group's name in the file

The matcher reads a `User-agent` value up to its first character that is
not a letter, `_` or `-`. So `User-agent: Googlebot/2.1` names the
`Googlebot` group, and `User-agent: Foo Bot` names `Foo`:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: Googlebot/2.1\nDisallow: /x\n", "/x", token = "Googlebot")
decide("User-agent: Foo Bot\nDisallow: /x\n", "/x", token = "Foo")
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 allows both: it compares the whole value, so neither
group applies. (Class 12.)

### Line endings

A carriage return alone ends a line:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\rDisallow: /x\r", "/x")
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 allows `/x` here, as if the file were one line. With
`\n` or `\r\n` line endings the two agree. RFC 9309 §2.2 counts a lone CR as
a line end. (Class 18.)

### Percent escapes

The matcher compares escapes as written. It does not decode `%2F` to `/`
or `%7E` to `~`:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /a%2Fb\n", c("/a/b", "/a%2Fb"))
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /%7Ejoe\n", c("/~joe", "/%7Ejoe"))
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 decodes escapes and disallows `/a/b` and `/~joe` too
(class 13). RFC 9309 §2.2.2 decodes `%7E` but keeps `%2F`, so on the
`%7E` row `robotstxt` follows the RFC and Google does not.

The matcher upper-cases a lower-case escape in a rule, but never in the
URL:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /a%3cb\n", c("/a%3cb", "/a%3Cb"))
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 disallows `/a%3cb`. (Class 14.)

### Raw non-ASCII and spaces

robotstxtr does not escape the URL. A raw `é` does not match an escaped
rule; the percent-encoded URL does:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /caf%C3%A9\n", c("/café", "/caf%C3%A9"))
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 escapes the URL first and disallows the raw form too
(class 15). If your paths hold raw non-ASCII characters, percent-encode
them before calling robotstxtr; `utils::URLencode()` is one way.

A raw space in a rule stays a raw space, so it does not match `%20`:

```{r}
decide("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /a b\n", c("/a%20b", "/a"))
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 disallows `/a%20b`. (Class 16.)

### Very long lines

The matcher reads at most 16,663 bytes of a line and cuts the rest, which
can leave a shorter rule that matches more:

```{r}
long_path <- paste0("/", strrep("a", 16700))
long_body <- paste0("User-agent: *\nDisallow: ", long_path, "/secret\n")
decide(long_body, paste0(long_path, "/public"))$allowed
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 allows this URL, since it reads the whole rule. The
validator reports such a line as `line_too_long`. (Class 17.)

### Byte order marks

robotstxtr skips one leading UTF-8 byte order mark. A second one stays part
of the first line, so `User-agent: *` below is not read and the rule has no
group:

```{r}
bom <- intToUtf8(0xFEFF)
decide(paste0(bom, bom, "User-agent: *\nDisallow: /a\n"), "/a")
```

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 disallows `/a`. (Class 3.)

### A line with an empty field name

`robotstxt` 0.7.15 stops with an error ("'names' attribute ... must be the
same length as the vector") on a file whose first field line has an empty
name, such as a line holding only `:`. robotstxtr ignores the line:

```{r}
decide(":\nUser-agent: *\nDisallow: /x\n", "/x")
```

(Errors and API constraints, `rtx` row.)

## What robotstxtr adds

### Search engine rulesets and matchers

`allowed_by_robots_text()` and `allowed_by_robots_url()` always use the
Google matcher. `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` and `robots_evaluate_url_v1()`
take two explicit choices instead:

- `robots_policy_ruleset`: how fetch evidence, such as a missing file, a
  server error or a redirect, becomes an action, per engine: `"google"`,
  `"yandex"`, `"bing"`, `"rfc9309"` or `"assumed_rfc9309"`.
- `matcher_backend`: which matcher reads the rules: `"google"`, `"yandex"`,
  `"bing"` or `"rfc9309"`.

```{r}
robots_engine_contract_v1()$matcher_availability
```

The `rfc9309` matcher is not built yet, and says so instead of falling back
to another matcher:

```{r}
robots_evaluate_text_v1(
  robots,
  "https://example.com/private/report",
  robots_product_token = "FooBot",
  robots_policy_ruleset = "rfc9309",
  matcher_backend = "rfc9309"
)$results[c("matcher_status", "reason", "url_decision")]
```

The Yandex and Bing matchers accept only the tokens they model, listed by
`robots_engine_contract_v1()$matcher_capability$<backend>$supported_profiles`
and checked with `robots_resolve_matcher_profile_v1()`:

```{r}
robots_evaluate_text_v1(
  robots,
  "https://example.com/private/report",
  robots_product_token = "bingbot",
  robots_policy_ruleset = "bing",
  matcher_backend = "bing"
)$results[c("matcher_status", "url_decision")]
```

`as_legacy_robots_decisions_v1()` turns a result evaluated with the Google
ruleset and matcher into the `robots_decisions` shape. The "Engine-aware
contract" vignette covers this interface in full.

### A validator

`robots_validate_text()` checks a file you hold, and
`robots_validate_url()` fetches and checks one. Several of the differences
above come from lines that the validator flags:

```{r}
v <- robots_validate_text(
  "User-agent: *\nDisallow: $\nDisallow: /a$*\nCrawl-delay: 5\n"
)
v$documents$validation_status
v$diagnostics[c("line", "severity", "code")]
```

The "Diagnostic codes" section of `?robots_validate_text` lists every code.

### A guarded fetch

Every request from `allowed_by_robots_url()`, `robots_fetch()`,
`robots_validate_url()` and `robots_evaluate_url_v1()` goes through the
`ssrfr` guard against server-side request forgery, for the first request
and for every redirect. A host that is, or resolves to, a loopback,
private, link-local or cloud-metadata address is refused before any
connection. The fetch also follows at most five redirects, refuses an
`https` to `http` redirect, sends no cookies or credentials, caps the body
at `max_bytes` (512 KiB by default) and has one `timeout` per origin.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Not evaluated here. The loopback origin is refused before any request:
# fetch_outcome is "ssrf_blocked", decision_source is "fetch_unknown" and
# allowed is NA.
allowed_by_robots_url("http://127.0.0.1/page", "FooBot")$results[
  c("fetch_outcome", "decision_source", "allowed")
]
```

`robotstxt` has no such guard, which matters when the URLs you check come
from users or from crawled pages.
